name: Amari Vitality membership packages design
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

Bethany is a marketing or business consultant who creates branded collateral, membership structures, and sales materials for medical spa clients. In this conversation, she worked on a comprehensive suite of documents for Amari Vitality, a medspa and wellness practice located in Cookeville, Tennessee that has a heritage in body sculpting and has expanded into full aesthetic and wellness services. A colleague named Natasha Jain was referenced as a stakeholder who provided input on naming conventions and simplification of membership benefits.

The work progressed through several iterations. Claude first built a table-based membership and package document, which Bethany redirected toward the prose-and-bullet format she uses with her other medspa clients, referencing prior Aesthetic Renewal collateral as the style template. Claude then produced three documents matching that established format: a Membership Collection with four tiers, a Signature Year annual program, and a Signature Packages document with four named packages (The Main Event, The Comeback, The Time Shift, The Vitality Reset). Natasha provided feedback renaming the tiers to Amari Signature, Amari Elite, Amari Prestige, and Amari Premier, and requesting simplified perks for easier front-desk selling and brochure use. Claude rebuilt the membership document accordingly. Bethany then provided a finalized word-for-word version of the membership collection with updated pricing (Signature $99, Elite $179, Prestige $249, VIP $459) and exact treatment selections, which Claude reproduced precisely without editorial changes. Claude also produced a formal membership agreement contract covering recurring billing authorization, Treatment Bank mechanics, cancellation, refunds, and medical discretion, with a recommendation that a Tennessee healthcare attorney review it before use. Finally, Claude built an in-treatment upsell and tier upgrade script organized into four parts: add-on offers by treatment type with exact spoken lines, a trigger table mapping consultation language to tier recommendations, word-for-word tier upgrade scripts, hesitation responses, and a checkout close.

Bethany's established working pattern is to receive complete, client-ready Word documents formatted for direct delivery, using a consistent visual style with brand color headers, gold accent rules, tab-aligned tier names with right-justified pricing, italic taglines, and gold-bordered quote callouts for spoken scripts. She uses this same structure across multiple client practices and expects Claude to match prior collateral rather than invent new formats. All documents follow her brand writing rules: no em dashes, formal language in written documents, and contractions used only in spoken scripts and casual communication. When she provides final copy marked as word-for-word, Claude reproduces it exactly and flags any discrepancies (such as mismatched pricing in estimated value lines) in the chat rather than correcting silently.

   406	## Editing Existing Documents
   407	
   408	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   409	
   410	### Step 1: Unpack
   411	```bash
   412	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   413	```
   414	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   415	
   416	### Step 2: Edit XML
   417	
   418	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   419	
   420	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   421	
   422	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   423	
   424	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   425	```xml
   426	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   427	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   428	```
   429	| Entity | Character |
   430	|--------|-----------|
   431	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   432	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   433	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   434	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   435	
   436	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   437	```bash
   438	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   439	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0

   441	```

   444	### Step 3: Pack
   445	```bash
   446	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   447	```

   449	
   450	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   451	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   452	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   453	
   454	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   455	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   456	
   457	### Common Pitfalls
   458	
   459	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.

   464	## XML Reference
   465	
   466	### Schema Compliance
   467	
   468	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   469	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   470	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   471	
   472	### Tracked Changes
   473	
   474	**Insertion:**
   475	```xml
   476	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   477	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   478	</w:ins>
   479	```
   480	
   481	**Deletion:**
   482	```xml
   483	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">

   485	</w:del>
   486	```

   488	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   489	
   490	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   491	```xml
   492	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   493	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   494	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   495	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   496	</w:del>
   497	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   498	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   499	</w:ins>
   500	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   501	```
   502	
   503	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   504	```xml
   505	<w:p>
   506	  <w:pPr>
   507	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   508	    <w:rPr>
   509	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   510	    </w:rPr>
   511	  </w:pPr>
   512	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   513	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   514	  </w:del>
   515	</w:p>
   516	```
   517	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   518	
   519	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   520	```xml
   521	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   522	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   523	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   524	  </w:del>
   525	</w:ins>
   526	```
   527	
   528	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   529	```xml
   530	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   531	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   532	</w:del>
   533	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   534	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   535	</w:ins>
   536	```

   538	### Comments
   539	
   540	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   541	
   542	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   543	
   544	```xml
   545	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   546	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   547	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   548	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   549	</w:del>
   550	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   551	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   552	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   553	
   554	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   555	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   556	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   557	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
   558	  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
   559	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   560	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   561	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
   562	```

   580	    <a:graphic>

   584	        </pic:pic>
   585	      </a:graphicData>
   586	    </a:graphic>
   587	  </wp:inline>
   588	</w:drawing>
   589	```

Here is the full client-facing collateral. It is built around four memberships (Glow, Signature, Elite, plus a Vitality Wellness track tied to her brand name) and six package collections, with the Sculpt Collection given the gold-header flagship treatment to honor the body sculpting heritage and pull in seasoned clients.

**The owner-side ROI logic (the part to keep internal)**

Memberships are priced as value-in-kind, not banked credit, which is what makes them so profitable. The Glow tier costs roughly $13 a month to deliver (a B-12 plus a quarterly basic facial) against a $99 fee. Signature costs about $35 to deliver against $199. Even Elite, the richest tier, runs around $90 against $349. Every membership clears 60 percent or better on the fee alone, before members spend a dollar at their discount, and they self-select into your highest-frequency clients.

The packages all hold strong margin because the bundled services have low supply cost:

- Sculpt Refine: roughly $950 cost on $2,999, about 68 percent margin
- Sculpt Transform: roughly $2,500 cost on $6,999, about 64 percent margin
- Total Body Reset: roughly $3,650 cost on $9,999, about 63 percent margin
- The Ageless Lift: roughly $700 cost on $2,999, about 77 percent margin
- Collagen Restore: roughly $300 cost on $2,199, about 86 percent margin

The body packages are where the Cookeville affordability concern is real, so I built in 3, 6, and 12-month payment plans. A $9,999 package at twelve months is $833 a month, which lands far more comfortably than a single five-figure invoice in that market.

**Two weakest parts, and stronger alternatives**

First, the Vitality Wellness Membership has a margin gap I want to flag honestly. At $129 it includes a follow-up visit ($75 value) plus a B-12 every month, and the real profit on weight management lives in the medication, which is a pass-through cost billed separately. As written, this tier is more of a retention and lead-gen tool than a profit center. A stronger version: raise it to $149 and include monthly lab review or a quarterly Glimpse scan, or restructure it so the membership fee is credited against the medication management fee rather than the visit. That keeps the sticky monthly cadence GLP-1 patients already have while protecting the spread.

Second, the injectable packages are the soft spot in the lineup. Filler and tox are unit-based and outcome-variable, so The Tox Club and Liquid Refresh feel thinner than the body and skin bundles. A stronger play is to drop the one-off bundles and run a single "Tox Loyalty" structure: every prepaid block earns the next treatment at a lower per-unit rate, which rewards frequency without locking a specific syringe count to a fixed price. That also dodges the awkward detail that her current-patient tox rate ($12) is higher than her new-patient rate ($10), which someone will eventually notice and ask about.

One thing to confirm before this goes to Donna's counterpart or to Amari: I used representative CoolSculpting areas (lower abdomen and flanks at $3,600) to build the Sculpt à la carte values. If the owner wants to anchor those packages to her full-abdomen or full-back pricing ($4,999), the perceived savings get even larger and you can hold the same investment price. Want me to build a second version anchored to the premium areas so she can pick the framing?

The agreement opens with a checkbox tier-selection table at the current pricing, then runs through 22 sections and closes with member signature, a separate payment authorization, and a practice representative block. I put initial-here lines on the four terms that protect Amari most: recurring billing, banked value expiration, the non-refundable clause, and clinical discretion. It is written to incorporate the Membership Collection brochure by reference, so you never have to re-sign the contract when a treatment on the menu changes.

**Please read this part before Natasha uses it.** I am not a lawyer, and a med spa membership sits on top of several areas of law that are worth an attorney's eyes, ideally a Tennessee healthcare attorney. The three I would flag specifically:

The recurring-billing and auto-renewal language should be checked against current Tennessee and federal recurring-payment rules, since a signed card-on-file authorization has disclosure requirements and those have been tightening. This is the single most common place these agreements get challenged.

The medical piece is the bigger one. Because a membership fee is being paid partly for medical treatments, states have rules about how a medical practice can bundle and discount services, who must own the entity, and how fees can be structured. An attorney should confirm the fee structure does not run into Tennessee's corporate-practice-of-medicine or fee-splitting rules, and that the person signing on behalf of the Practice has the authority to do so.

A few numbers inside are policy choices I picked reasonable defaults for, and Natasha should confirm she actually wants them: the 30-day window to use banked value after cancellation, the 30-day written cancellation notice, the one-to-three-month pause range, and forfeiture of banked value on non-payment. Any of those can be made more generous or stricter, and I can adjust in a minute once she decides.

One gap worth closing separately: this is the membership contract, not the per-treatment informed consent. The agreement points to those consents in Sections 9 and 19, but Amari still needs individual consent forms for the actual procedures (tox, filler, CoolSculpting, laser, and so on). The script is built in four parts the team can work straight through.

Part 1 gives the exact add-on to offer during each treatment and the words to say, drawn from Amari's real add-on menu: LED, hydro jelly, and perks during facials, a B-12 or lip flip during injectables, PHYSIQ and Everesse during body contouring, a PRP upgrade during microneedling, a second area during laser, and boosts or peptides during IV and wellness. Every spoken line is set off in a gold callout so a provider can find it at a glance.

Part 2 is the tier-upgrade engine. There is a trigger table that maps what the client says in her consultation to the tier that serves her, then word-for-word scripts for each move, Signature to Elite, Elite to Prestige, and Prestige to VIP, plus the "let the math close it" move where the team adds up her treatment and add-ons and shows her that it already exceeds the next tier's monthly fee. It closes with where to start a brand new client.

Parts 3 and 4 handle the three most common hesitations and the checkout close, ending on the one habit that drives retention: never let a client pay full price for something a membership would have made cheaper without showing her the membership first.

Two things worth flagging so the team uses this cleanly and stays out of trouble:

The tier scripts lean on the "it pays for itself the first visit" line, which is true when the client is genuinely buying add-ons, but if the team says it reflexively to someone who only came for one facial, it stops being true and starts sounding like a pitch. I wrote the math section to prevent that, but it is worth telling the team plainly in training: only say "it pays for itself" after you have an actual number that proves it.

The injectable add-on lines, especially offering a second area "while you are already numb," need a guardrail. Any added tox or filler is a medical decision that requires the provider's sign-off and a consent for the new area, not just a yes in the chair. I would have the front desk and estheticians tee those up as "let me have your injector take a look," rather than committing to the add-on themselves.
